cards.headline: One stock is a bet. A portfolio is a plan.
cards.body: A portfolio is everything you own, held together. The point is not to pick the single winner — it is to arrange many holdings so that no one mistake can sink you.

cards.headline: Don't put it all in one basket.
cards.body: **Diversification** means spreading money across many investments, so that if one loses, the others can cushion the blow. It is the closest thing investing has to a free lunch.

cards.title: A sample allocation
cards.caption: **Asset allocation** is how you split money across stocks, bonds, and cash. A longer time horizon usually means more in stocks; a shorter one, less.

cards.headline: Allocation drives your risk.
cards.body: The split between stocks, bonds, and cash shapes your risk more than any single pick does. It follows two things: your **time horizon**, and how large a fall you can actually stomach.
Real diversification spreads risk along three different lines, not just across a handful of names.

cards.prompt: You own 20 technology stocks. Are you well diversified?

options.label: Yes — twenty is a lot of stocks
No — they can all fall together

cards.explanation: Twenty names in one **sector** still tend to rise and fall together. Diversification is about holding things that do not move in lockstep — not simply holding many things.

cards.headline: Winners drift your mix.
cards.body: Over time your best performers grow into an outsized share of the portfolio. **Rebalancing** trims them back toward your targets — a built-in habit of selling a little high and buying a little low.
Diversification can lower your risk, but it can never fully [[1]] it.
cards.explanation: Spreading out cuts the risk tied to any one company. But when the whole market falls, most things fall with it — and that shared risk stays.

cards.headline: What it can't do.
cards.body: Diversification tames company-specific risk, not market-wide risk. In a broad crash most assets drop together. Owning more names softens the blow; it does not make a portfolio crash-proof.

cards.summary: A portfolio spreads your money on purpose, so no single loss can undo you — then rebalances to stay that way.
bullets: Diversify across companies, sectors, and asset types.
Allocation — your stock, bond, and cash mix — sets your risk.
Rebalance back to target as winners drift the mix.

cards.insight: You cannot reliably pick the one winner. You can decide how much of any single loss you are willing to feel.

sources.title: Beginners' Guide to Asset Allocation, Diversification, and Rebalancing
